description: We are tackling “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.”
summary:
We developed LUNAR-TWIN, an open-source, two-way regional topographic analog finder (Moon → Earth and Earth → Moon) deployed as an interactive Streamlit web application. Historically, terrestrial test sites like the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, and Iceland have been chosen by habit and visual resemblance, yet looking alike is not driving alike.   

To address the challenge quantitatively, LUNAR-TWIN applies an identical spherical 3×3 stencil at a unified 1,895.2 m baseline to NASA PDS LRO LOLA (LDEM_16) and ESA Copernicus (GLO-90) elevation data, comparing Horn slope and plane-detrended RMS roughness across 16,200 lunar cells and 16 terrestrial zones (7 benchmarks and 9 candidates, including Harrat Khaybar and Vietnam's Krong No basalt field). It integrates NASA POWER climatology to penalize terrestrial moisture and rainfall, validates rankings via 300 Monte Carlo weight-perturbation runs, and pairs every match with a "Where the Analogy Breaks Down" audit.   

With nine Artemis III candidate regions within 6° of the lunar south pole and an 8° lander tilt limit, LUNAR-TWIN gives mission teams a repeatable, scientifically transparent shortlist for rover mobility testing—explicitly distinguishing true geometric matches from non-reproducible lunar physics like 1/6 g gravity, hard vacuum, and polar sensor gaps.
details:
1. High-Level Summary

We developed LUNAR-TWIN, an open-source, two-way topographic analog finder (Moon ↔ Earth) built with Streamlit. Traditionally, terrestrial rover test sites like the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, and Iceland are chosen by habit and visual appearance, yet looking alike does not mean driving alike.

LUNAR-TWIN applies the exact same metric code and length scale to NASA LRO LOLA and ESA Copernicus elevation data, comparing slope and surface roughness across 16,200 lunar cells and 16 Earth zones (7 established benchmarks and 9 candidate regions, including Harrat Khaybar and Vietnam's Krong No lava field). It penalizes terrestrial moisture using NASA POWER data, tests ranking stability, and highlights where Earth comparisons break down—giving mission teams a transparent, repeatable shortlist for rover mobility testing.

2. Project Details

What It Does & How It Works

LUNAR-TWIN is an interactive web application that searches for terrain matches in both directions:

  • Moon → Earth: Pick a lunar landing site or coordinate to rank the closest Earth training sites by slope, surface roughness, and aridity.
  • Earth → Moon: Pick an accessible field site on Earth to see which of the Moon's 16,200 regional cells match its terrain geometry.
  • The Same Ruler on Both Worlds: Both pipelines run identical spherical geometry code at a unified ~1.9 km baseline using NASA PDS LRO LOLA elevation data for the Moon and ESA Copernicus DEM + NASA POWER climate data for Earth.

Key Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Data-Driven Rover Testbed Selection: NASA's nine candidate Artemis III regions all sit near the lunar south pole, where an 8-degree slope limit governs lander safety and rover mobility. Our tool replaces reputation-based site selection with repeatable, open-data screening.
  • Validated Discoveries: Known analog benchmarks (such as Atacama, Haughton Crater, and Craters of the Moon) rank high as a sanity check, while our top candidate match for the Apollo 11 terrain is the Harrat Khaybar Basalt Field (Saudi Arabia) with a 93.0 similarity index and 100% top-3 stability.
  • Interactive Weight Testing: Users can adjust sliders for slope, roughness, and moisture penalties in real time, backed by 300 automated sensitivity runs to verify ranking stability.

How It Is Creative & Factors Considered

  • Explicit "Where the Analogy Breaks Down" Audit: Instead of over-claiming similarity, every match displays a side-by-side audit contrasting what matches (regional slope and roughness) against what no Earth site can reproduce: lunar 1/6 g gravity, hard vacuum, extreme temperature swings, radiation, and meter-scale hazards.
  • Strict Scientific Integrity: Our data audit revealed that LRO Diviner rock and thermal maps stop around 60–70° latitude and do not cover polar Artemis sites beyond 84° S. Rather than inventing extrapolated values, we report polar thermal/soil gaps transparently and score only verified terrain data.
  • Global & Local Coverage: Alongside major arid volcanic zones worldwide, we evaluated Krong No Basalt and Lava Tubes (Vietnam) to test Southeast Asian volcanic terrain against lunar benchmarks.

Tools & Software Used

  • Data Sources: NASA PDS LRO LOLA (Global Elevation, Slope, and Roughness), NASA LRO Diviner (audited for rock/thermal coverage limits), NASA POWER Climatology API, and ESA Copernicus DEM / Sentinel-1 & Sentinel-2.
  • Tech Stack: Python, Streamlit, Plotly, NumPy, SciPy, and Pandas, developed on Google Colab and local laptops.
